summary: Defines a way to encrypt data in the Cryptographic Message Syntax using a user-supplied password or other variable-length secret. Before this, the format had no provision for password-based encryption. It was replaced by RFC 3369 and RFC 3370.

eli5.summary: Normally a lock needs a special metal key. This lets you lock a message with a password you remember instead. It has been replaced by RFC 3369 and RFC 3370.

subtitle: A fourth way to wrap a message's encryption key in CMS: derive a key-encryption key from a password.

tldr.problem: The Cryptographic Message Syntax had no provision for encrypting data with a user-supplied password or other variable-length keying material.
tldr.mechanism: A new recipient type, PasswordRecipientInfo, derives a key-encryption key from the password (PBKDF2 is mandatory) and uses a double-encryption key wrap to protect the content-encryption key.
tldr.outcome: Proposed Standard in 2001, now replaced by RFC 3369 and RFC 3370. Security rests on the password's entropy, which is typically low.

today: RFC 3211 was obsoleted by RFC 3369 and RFC 3370, so those are the current CMS specifications rather than this one.

sections.title: A Fourth Recipient Type
sections.content:
CMS already defined three recipient information types: key transport (KeyTransRecipientInfo), conventional key wrapping (KEKRecipientInfo) and key agreement (KeyAgreeRecipientInfo). This RFC adds a fourth, PasswordRecipientInfo, for password-based key wrapping, and extends the RecipientInfo choice with it as pwri [3].

Although it is described in terms of passwords, the transformation is a general key derivation step that can turn any keying material into a key for a particular content-encryption algorithm. The RFC notes that the word "recipient" is somewhat misleading, since password encryption is mostly used on locally stored files, but the term is kept because the other mechanisms are described the same way.
sections.eli5: The message format already had three ways to hand over the secret key. This adds a fourth: let the person type a password instead.

sections.title: The PasswordRecipientInfo Structure
sections.content:
The structure has four fields. version MUST be 0. keyDerivationAlgorithm is optional and identifies how the key-encryption key (KEK) is derived from the password; if it is absent, the KEK comes from an external source such as a smart card. keyEncryptionAlgorithm identifies the algorithm that encrypts the content-encryption key (CEK) with the KEK. encryptedKey holds the result.

Wrapping is a two-stage process: first the password becomes a KEK, then the KEK encrypts the CEK. The two stages get separate algorithm identifiers because the combined single-identifier design of PKCS #5 version 2 (RFC 2898) may not suit other key wrapping mechanisms.

The format cannot tell multiple password recipients apart, for example when two passwords encrypt the same data. The RFC says there is too little existing practice to define this well, and leaves it to a possible future version.
sections.eli5: The package says which recipe turns your password into a key, which recipe locks the secret key with it, and then holds the locked secret key.

sections.title: Required Algorithms
sections.content:
Conforming implementations MUST include PBKDF2 for key derivation. For key encryption, the algorithm identifier is id-alg-PWRI-KEK, whose parameters name the KEK encryption algorithm used with the key wrap of the next section. Implementations MUST implement this wrap and MUST include Triple-DES in CBC mode. They MAY include others such as AES, CAST-128, RC5, IDEA, Skipjack and Blowfish.

Implementations SHOULD NOT include keystream generator ciphers such as RC4 or a block cipher in OFB mode, and SHOULD NOT include a block cipher in ECB mode. The CEK algorithm need not match the KEK algorithm, but they should offer equivalent security; wrapping a Triple-DES key with an RC2/40 key is the RFC's example of a severe mismatch.

The parameters field is left explicit with no default, because of confusion over NULL versus absent parameters in algorithm identifiers.
sections.eli5: Everyone must know at least one standard way to stretch a password into a key and one standard lock. Some old kinds of locks are advised against.

sections.title: Key Wrap and Unwrap
sections.content:
The key wrap has two phases. In formatting, the CEK is placed in a block made of a one-byte count of the CEK bytes, a check value (the bitwise complement of the first three CEK bytes), the CEK, and random padding. The padding makes the block a multiple of the KEK block length and at least two cipher blocks long. PKCS #5 padding is not used.

In wrapping, the formatted block is encrypted with the KEK, then, without resetting the IV, encrypted a second time. The double-encrypted result is the EncryptedKey.

To unwrap, the receiver decrypts the last block using the previous ciphertext block as the IV, then the earlier blocks using that result as the IV, which strips the outer layer. The inner layer is decrypted with the KEK. The receiver then checks the count and the check value; if either is wrong, the KEK was invalid, meaning the password was wrong.

The double wrap makes every ciphertext bit depend on every CEK bit. This avoids block collisions when many CEKs are wrapped with the same 64-bit-block KEK (a high chance after about 2^32 encryptions), resists bit-flipping, gives a different result each time because the IV is applied to the inner layer, and needs no extra hash algorithm, which suits devices such as smart cards.
sections.eli5: The secret key is packed with a label and a checksum, locked once, and then locked again. If your password is wrong, the checksum will not match when it is unpacked.

sections.title: Test Vectors
sections.content:
The RFC includes two sets of test vectors. The basic set uses DES and is built to verify correctness with an algorithm that was freely exportable from the US. It derives a DES-CBC key from the password password with an 8-byte salt using 5 iterations of PBKDF2, and includes a known-answer test of the derivation stage and a full test of wrapping a 64-bit DES key.

The second set is a stress test with a very long passphrase, a 256-bit key and Triple-DES, using 500 iterations of PBKDF2, to verify behavior in extreme cases. A worked example in the wrap section shows a Skipjack CEK wrapped with Triple-DES.
sections.eli5: The RFC gives worked answers so builders can check that their code gets exactly the same result as everyone else's.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
Security rests on the underlying mechanisms in CMS and PKCS #5 version 2, and, more importantly, on the entropy of the user-selected password, which is typically quite low. Pass phrases rather than simple passwords are STRONGLY RECOMMENDED.

The RFC also warns that even with pass phrases it will be difficult to derive a KEK with enough entropy to properly protect a 128-bit or longer CEK.

A strong cipher does not help if the password is easy to guess.
sections.eli5: A great lock is useless if your password is easy to guess, so use a long phrase instead of a short word.
